currentContext.expansion: SJVN's stated growth roadmap is to scale installed capacity to 25,000 MW by 2030 and to become a 50,000+ MW company by 2040, through a Business Development Plan for 2025-2030 building a balanced portfolio supporting base load (hydro), peak load (pumped storage) and variable demand (solar/wind + storage). Present installed capacity is 4196.5 MW across 15 operational power stations with 3926.5 MW under construction, plus a long-term development pipeline of projects aggregating 5,693 MW spread across India and Nepal. In hydro, the plan is to fast-track execution of major under-construction projects - 210 MW Luhri Stage-I, 66 MW Dhaulasidh and 382 MW Sunni Dam - alongside an MoU signed for the 680 MW Attunli HEP in Arunachal Pradesh (projects at different stages of clearances); the 900 MW Arun-3 HEP in Nepal has progressed across civil, hydro-mechanical, electro-mechanical and transmission works and is significantly closer to commissioning. Strategic tie-ups with state governments are intended to unlock stalled projects, with international ventures in Nepal and Bhutan to be explored. SJVN has signed an MoU for the 1800 MW Kotpali Pumped Storage Project in Chhattisgarh, is in process for taking over hydro projects on the Arun River and other valleys, and a draft Joint Venture Agreement for the 900 MW GMR Upper Karnali HEP in Nepal is under finalisation with the Nepal Electricity Authority. In renewables, developed through wholly owned subsidiary SJVN Green Energy Limited (SGEL), SJVN aims to add 10-12 GW of solar and wind capacity by 2030 via ultra-mega solar parks (UMREPPs), SECI and state RE auctions, hybrid and floating solar, focused on Rajasthan, Gujarat and Maharashtra for solar and Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh for wind, plus captive solar and third-party sale under green open access. SGEL has 1460 MW of projects under operation; 855 MW is under construction (Bagodra 70 MW Gujarat, COD March-2027; GUVNL Phase-XIII 100 MW Gujarat, June-2027; GUVNL Phase-XIV 260 MW Gujarat, June-2027; Jamui Phase-I 75 MW Bihar, July 2026; APDCL 50 MW Assam, July 2026; GUVNL Phase-XVII Khavda 200 MW Gujarat, Dec 2026; RUVNL Nawa 100 MW Rajasthan, Sep 2026) and 1500 MW is under pre-construction (PSPSCL ET-2 100 MW Punjab, March 2027; PSPSCL ET-4 200 MW Punjab, March 2027; PSPSCL ET-3 1000 MW Pan India, March 2027; APDCL 200 MW Assam, December 2027). Under GUVNL Phase-XXII SJVN has secured a 200 MW solar project in Gujarat with a PPA at Rs 2.63/kWh signed by SGEL on 09.04.2024 and financial closure achieved; EPC awards have been placed for 150 MW and the remaining 50 MW is at tendering stage and yet to be awarded (the section heading in the report labels this item '50 MW' while the body states 200 MW secured). In thermal, one 660 MW unit of the 1320 MW Buxar Thermal Power Project (STPL) was commissioned on 14.11.2025 and Unit-II is expected to be commissioned during FY 2026-27. In green hydrogen, SJVN will establish pilot-scale hydrogen production using dedicated solar power especially in arid regions, with a 10-20 TPD demonstration facility and future scaling based on commercial viability, and has been nominated by the Ministry of Power as nodal agency for a green hydrogen project in Nepal. risks.risk: Hydrological variability and reduced water availability (BRSR material issue #1, Risk)
risks.note: Changes in precipitation patterns, glacier melt dynamics and prolonged dry periods from climate change may alter the timing and volume of river flows, reducing water available for hydroelectric generation and hitting operational efficiency and generation capacity. Stated financial implications are negative: reduced inflows lower electricity generation and revenue, fixed operating costs continue despite lower generation, and variability increases sediment-management needs and periodic reductions in plant utilisation. Mitigation is reservoir optimisation, storage enhancement, integrated water resource planning and monitoring of climatic/hydrological trends. The MD&A separately flags dependence on rainfall, solar radiation and wind resources as a weakness exposing the Company to weather-related uncertainty.

risks.risk: Climate change physical and transition risk (BRSR material issue #2, Risk & Opportunity)
risks.note: Operations may be affected by climate-induced changes in rainfall patterns, snowmelt timing and glacial retreat; floods, droughts and landslides may damage infrastructure and raise O&M costs. Negative implications stated: lower generation during droughts or altered rainfall can impact plant load factor and earnings, plus costs of new climate disclosure mandates, carbon footprint monitoring and retrofitting. Offsetting positives: eligibility for climate finance, green bonds and concessional funding, and improved investor confidence potentially reducing cost of capital. Mitigation is comprehensive ESIAs and an Environment Management Plan.

risks.risk: Erosion of hydro's competitive position as solar and wind tariffs fall, and PPA risk
risks.note: MD&A threats state that with solar and wind tariffs declining, the viability of hydro power - SJVN's core strength - is becoming increasingly questionable, and that a technological breakthrough making battery storage economically and sustainably viable may make hydro generation unviable. New hydro projects carry higher tariff in the initial years and struggle to compete with cheaper renewables and thermal. Compounding this: beneficiaries not signing PPAs for new hydro projects and disowning signed PPAs where project tariff is high, and declining wind/solar tariffs constraining renewal or extension of PPAs for existing projects - explicitly described as a risk to future revenues.

risks.risk: Geological surprises, remote-site natural calamities and construction execution risk
risks.note: Most hydro-electric projects are in remote locations prone to cloud burst, landslide and road blockage, contributing to delays, unforeseen events and cost escalation. Despite extensive survey and investigation, the probability of geological surprises in components of hydro projects in the young Himalayan ranges poses a technical challenge involving extremely cost-intensive and time-consuming measures; hydro projects are vulnerable to geological uncertainties and site-specific challenges that can cause time and cost overruns, raising project costs and hence tariffs.

risks.risk: Clearance, approval and regulatory-compliance risk (BRSR material issue #9, Risk & Opportunity)
risks.note: Stringent norms and cumbersome procedures for environment clearance, forest clearance, National Board for Wild Life clearance and land acquisition delay the commencement of construction. Hydropower projects require approvals under multiple laws including the Environmental Protection Act, Electricity Act and Labour Codes, increasing the risk of non-compliance; compliance-related adjustments may occasionally cause operational slowdowns. The opportunity side: a strong compliance record may facilitate faster clearances, access to incentives and preferred treatment under renewable energy policies, plus access to green financing and government grants.

risks.risk: Rehabilitation & Resettlement and community/social licence risk (BRSR material issue #6, Risk)
risks.note: Large hydropower projects may require relocating families, affecting livelihoods, access to natural resources and cultural ties, which may lead to resistance or unrest. Inadequate R&R planning, non-compliance with statutory guidelines or improper handling of land rights may result in litigation or project suspension; community resistance or legal challenges may cause project delays and substantially increase costs, and non-compliance may result in fines, court-mandated rehabilitation measures or forced project stoppages.

risks.risk: Biodiversity and habitat impact risk (BRSR material issue #4, Risk)
risks.note: Dam construction, reservoir creation and alterations in river flow regimes may impact habitats, aquatic species, migratory patterns and endemic flora and fauna; perceived or actual impacts on biodiversity hotspots, protected areas or indigenous lands may attract opposition from NGOs and communities. Delays in securing environmental and biodiversity clearances may cause time and cost overruns, and non-compliance with biodiversity laws may lead to legal fines or project suspension. Mitigated through a Biodiversity Management Plan and CSR initiatives on biodiversity conservation.

risks.risk: Occupational health & safety, and human rights / contract-labour risk (BRSR material issues #7 and #5, Risk)
risks.note: Activities involving large dams, turbines and electrical systems expose workers to falls, electrocution and equipment-related injuries, and SJVN plants sit in remote mountainous regions susceptible to floods, landslides and earthquakes. Unsafe conditions may attract media scrutiny, diminish community trust and adversely affect investor sentiment, while safety incidents may interrupt project activities and cause cost overruns and revenue losses. Separately, mismanagement of contract labour, wage disputes or unsafe working conditions may result in unrest, strikes or legal proceedings, and failure to comply with human rights laws or labour codes may bring regulatory penalties and investor scrutiny; mitigation via Corporate HR ownership, project-level Internal Compliance Committees, PPE, risk assessments, training and site inspections.

risks.risk: Asset and policy concentration: cascade dependency, state hydro policy changes and project allotment
risks.note: NJHPS and RHPS are cascade schemes operating in tandem, so any difficulty in NJHPS operation has direct consequences for RHPS generation - a structural single-basin concentration in the company's largest earning assets. State governments may change hydro policy by introducing Water Cess, Land Cess or enhanced free power, and there is reluctance of state governments to allot hydro/PSP projects, constraining the growth pipeline.

risks.risk: Business ethics / governance conduct risk (BRSR material issue #11, Risk)
risks.note: Bribes, favouritism in land acquisition or misreporting of environmental impacts may result in scandals, and regulatory authorities may revoke or delay approvals if unethical conduct is identified; fines, compensation claims and court-related expenses arising from unethical conduct may significantly affect financial stability. Mitigation asserted is compliance with all applicable legal and regulatory requirements.

risks.risk: Risk-management framework dependency (BRSR material issue #10, Risk)
risks.note: In the absence of a robust risk management framework the Company may be exposed to natural disasters, policy changes and technical failures, and non-compliance arising from inadequate monitoring or limited foresight may create financial and reputational risks; legal expenses, regulatory fines and compensation payments may impose significant financial burdens, and revenue losses from operational downtime may further affect long-term profitability. Mitigation is a Board-approved Risk Management Policy (September 2022), an ISO 31000:2018 framework with project- and corporate-level Risk Steering Committees (quarterly and half-yearly respectively), Board-level Risk Management Committee meetings once in six months, and an annual external Risk Audit for ISO 31000:2018 compliance.

- **PPA cancellation risk:** ~9-10 GW awarded-but-unsigned at risk; DISCOM demand/config mismatch + falling tariffs.

non-obvious takeaways:
- The +308% Q4 PAT and +22% FY revenue are largely **non-recurring true-up artifacts** — not a clean growth signal.
- The growth story has **structurally downshifted**: from a 25 GW-by-2030 aspirant to a "consolidate what we have" posture. Re-rating thesis must be reset.
- SJVN's loss-making thermal/solar is a **timing problem** (PLF/CUF ramp + pre-COD cost charging), not necessarily a structural one — FY27 is the proof point.
- The REIA/aggregator model exposes SJVN to **DISCOM demand risk** it doesn't fully control — awarded GW ≠ contracted GW.
- Grid-balancing equipment (SVR reactors) is a **single-point bottleneck** ("limited manufacturer") capping solar output — a sector-wide integration constraint as solar penetration rises.

- Solar: lower CUF on some plants + new-asset finance cost & depreciation charged before full ramp.
- Incentives FY26: secondary energy +20%; PAF -23%; deviation -3%. Q4: secondary energy +16%; PAF-incentive -40%; deviation 0%.
capex / expansion:
- CAPEX INR 9,400 cr (current yr), INR 7,800 cr (FY28), INR 7,500 cr (FY29).
- Heavy under-construction book of 3,926.5 MW; funding question raised by analyst but mgmt deflected to the broader business-plan reset rather than a specific debt/equity mix.
capital allocation:
- **Dividend FY26:** total 15% on INR 10 face value = **INR 1.50/share** (interim INR 1.15 + final INR 0.35). Standard CPSE payout discipline.
- Capital being redirected from over-ambitious 25/50 GW vision toward consolidating existing commissioned/under-construction assets and improving their utilization.
risks & watch-items:
- **Quality of earnings:** FY26 PAT flattered by INR 679 cr prior-period true-up; underlying growth far lower than headline +22% revenue / +4% PAT suggests.
- **Receivables blow-up:** Trade receivables jumped to INR 1,299 cr (from INR 262 cr), unbilled debtors INR 906 cr (incl INR 776 cr tariff-order billing slipping into FY27) — working-capital and realization risk.
- **PPA cancellation risk:** ~9-10 GW awarded-but-unsigned at risk; DISCOM demand/config mismatch + falling tariffs.
- **Curtailment:** Bikaner ~120 MW curtailed pending SVR reactor (Oct-26); Khavda/Gujarat ~300 MW curtailment risk from delayed transmission/connectivity.
- **Loss-making subsidiaries** (SGEL, STPL) dragging consol; turnaround entirely dependent on FY27 ramp execution.
- **Tax step-up:** Sec 80-IA holiday expired for Rampur & KWPP → structurally higher tax.
- **Forex:** INR 206 cr exchange-variation hit (Nepal/external borrowing exposure).
- **Execution/geology:** Nepal hydro history of delays.
management quality / tone: Candid and specific — Director Finance gave granular subsidiary P&L; CMD openly admitted the 25/50 GW vision was unrealistic ("projects did not come in time", tenders did not materialize) and is being reset. Tone is sober/realistic rather than promotional, which is a positive on credibility but a negative on near-term growth optics. Repeatedly hedged on PPA conversion ("very, very difficult to say").
non-obvious takeaways:
- The +308% Q4 PAT and +22% FY revenue are largely **non-recurring true-up artifacts** — not a clean growth signal.
- The growth story has **structurally downshifted**: from a 25 GW-by-2030 aspirant to a "consolidate what we have" posture. Re-rating thesis must be reset.
- SJVN's loss-making thermal/solar is a **timing problem** (PLF/CUF ramp + pre-COD cost charging), not necessarily a structural one — FY27 is the proof point.
- The REIA/aggregator model exposes SJVN to **DISCOM demand risk** it doesn't fully control — awarded GW ≠ contracted GW.
- Grid-balancing equipment (SVR reactors) is a **single-point bottleneck** ("limited manufacturer") capping solar output — a sector-wide integration constraint as solar penetration rises.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- All-India installed power generation capacity was 537264.37 MW as on 30.04.2026, with 64695 MW added in FY 2025-26 (9470 MW thermal, 3620 MW large hydro, 700 MW nuclear, 50,905 MW other renewables) - management reads this as ample opportunity for consistent growth in hydro, PSP, renewable and thermal energy sectors.
- India met an all-time maximum power demand of 242.49 GW during FY 2025-26 and national energy shortage fell to an all-time low of 0.03%; the National Electricity Plan 2023-2032 targets meeting a peak demand of 458 GW by 2032.
- Per capita electricity consumption rose to 1460 kWh in 2024-25, a 52.6% increase from 957 kWh in 2013-14; rural power availability up from 12.5 hours (2014) to 22.6 hours and urban to 23.4 hours.
- Large unharnessed hydro potential: India's estimated hydro potential is about 133410 MW of which only about 51415 MW (including PSP as on 31.03.2026) is commissioned, with the bulk located in Arunachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, Sikkim and Jammu & Kashmir.
- Pumped storage as 'water batteries': India's PSP potential is about 267 GW (58 GW on-stream, 209 GW off-stream), only 7 GW developed and 12 GW under construction; the Government target is 100 GW or more of pumped storage capacity by 2035-36.
- India's goal of 500 GW non-fossil energy capacity by 2030 and Net Zero by 2070; India has already crossed over 50% of installed electricity capacity from non-fossil sources, five years ahead of its NDC target.
- Government initiatives creating a favourable environment for capacity expansion: Hydro Purchase Obligation, tariff rationalisation for legacy hydropower projects, budgetary support for enabling infrastructure in Himalayan and North-Eastern States, and renewed focus on PSPs.
- Hydropower's grid balancing, peaking support and storage role is increasingly recognised as the ideal complement to India's rapidly growing solar and wind capacity; with fast growth in solar, hydro's peaking power has huge potential to contribute to grid stability.
- Energy security narrative: recent tensions in West Asia and evolving geopolitical developments have highlighted self-reliance and energy security; accelerating clean energy transition, efficiency, domestic manufacturing and grid modernisation reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels (Atmanirbhar Bharat).
- Regulated revenue model is a stability driver: NJHPS and RHPS tariffs are CERC-determined under Tariff Regulations 2024 (effective 01.04.2024 for five years); Annual Fixed Charges comprise ROE (grossed up for tax), depreciation, interest on loan, interest on working capital and O&M, split equally into energy charges and capacity charges, with incentives for PAF above the Normative Annual Plant Availability Factor and secondary energy charges for generation above design energy.
- Tariff overhang: the CERC tariff order for NJHPS w.e.f. 1 April 2024 is still pending, so NJHPS billing is provisional at the tariff applicable as on 31 March 2024.
- Margin/viability headwind flagged: with tariffs of solar and wind projects falling, the viability of hydro power projects - SJVN's core strength - is becoming increasingly questionable; new hydro projects carry higher tariff in initial years and are hard to compete against cheaper renewables and thermal.
- PPA risk: non-signing of PPAs by beneficiaries for new hydro projects and disowning of signed PPAs where project tariff is high; declining wind/solar tariffs may constrain renewal or extension of PPAs for existing projects, posing a risk to future revenues.
- Policy risk: changes in hydro policy by state governments introducing water cess, land cess and enhanced free power; reluctance of state governments to allot hydro/PSP projects.
- Resource and execution dependence: reliance on rainfall, solar radiation and wind resources creates weather-related uncertainty for generation and revenue; hydro projects face geological uncertainties, remote locations prone to cloud burst/landslide, and clearance delays (environment, forest, National Board for Wildlife, land acquisition) that drive time and cost overruns.
- Technology risk: a technological breakthrough making battery storage for renewable energy economically and sustainably viable may make hydro power generation unviable.
- Cascade dependency: NJHPS and RHPS are cascade schemes operating in tandem, so any difficulty in NJHPS operation directly affects RHPS generation.
- Adjacent market pipelines cited as demand support: India's storage tender pipeline of ~13 GWh by 2030, a target of 5 MMT green hydrogen production by 2030, and plans to tender 4 GW of offshore wind by 2026 backed by international financing; transmission is a bottleneck for renewable expansion.
- SJVN's own growth base: present installed capacity 4196.5 MW with 3926.5 MW under construction, expected to generate strong cash flows and propel growth.
- REIA pipeline (FY 2025-26): tenders floated for a cumulative capacity of 3.45 GW; Letters of Award issued to successful developers for a cumulative capacity of 4.373 GW during FY 2025-26.
- REIA cumulative to date: tenders floated for a total capacity of 22.425 GW, of which LoAs have been issued for a total capacity of 16.023 GW; a further cumulative capacity of 2.6 GW is currently under the tendering process and is expected to be concluded by July 2026.
- REIA Power Sale Agreements: PSAs executed with DISCOMs/States for an awarded capacity of 5.915 GW to date across FDRE, solar, wind and BESS, of which 2.177 GW of PSAs were signed during FY 2025-26; PSAs for the remaining awarded capacity of 10.108 GW are expected to be signed shortly.
- Rooftop solar (PM Surya Ghar): baseline assessments and tendering completed for 29.2 MW across Union Government buildings PAN-India under the RESCO model, plus 1 MW in Arunachal Pradesh under the CAPEX model.
- Rooftop solar execution: 17 Power Purchase Agreements signed aggregating 2.49 MW, under implementation in Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Gujarat, plus the rooftop project at the Arunachal Pradesh State Government Secretariat building.
- Rooftop solar pipeline: Letters of Award issued for 15.99 MW across Delhi, Maharashtra, West Bengal, Karnataka, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Assam and Odisha in addition to ongoing states; another 5.26 MW under advanced stages of techno-commercial evaluation.
- Power trading: PPA signed with wholly owned subsidiary STPL for sale of 15% of unallocated power to Power Exchanges/bilateral; Letter of Award received from NTPC Vidyut Vyapar Nigam Limited (NVVN) for procurement of up to 200 MW of power through the SJVN Power Trading Department.
- Power trading cumulative volume from commencement of the business up to 31st March 2026: 230 MU.
- Construction pipeline: fifteen projects totalling 3926.5 MW under construction against present installed capacity of 4196.5 MW.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: SJVN's stated growth roadmap is to scale installed capacity to 25,000 MW by 2030 and to become a 50,000+ MW company by 2040, through a Business Development Plan for 2025-2030 building a balanced portfolio supporting base load (hydro), peak load (pumped storage) and variable demand (solar/wind + storage). Present installed capacity is 4196.5 MW across 15 operational power stations with 3926.5 MW under construction, plus a long-term development pipeline of projects aggregating 5,693 MW spread across India and Nepal. In hydro, the plan is to fast-track execution of major under-construction projects - 210 MW Luhri Stage-I, 66 MW Dhaulasidh and 382 MW Sunni Dam - alongside an MoU signed for the 680 MW Attunli HEP in Arunachal Pradesh (projects at different stages of clearances); the 900 MW Arun-3 HEP in Nepal has progressed across civil, hydro-mechanical, electro-mechanical and transmission works and is significantly closer to commissioning. Strategic tie-ups with state governments are intended to unlock stalled projects, with international ventures in Nepal and Bhutan to be explored. SJVN has signed an MoU for the 1800 MW Kotpali Pumped Storage Project in Chhattisgarh, is in process for taking over hydro projects on the Arun River and other valleys, and a draft Joint Venture Agreement for the 900 MW GMR Upper Karnali HEP in Nepal is under finalisation with the Nepal Electricity Authority. In renewables, developed through wholly owned subsidiary SJVN Green Energy Limited (SGEL), SJVN aims to add 10-12 GW of solar and wind capacity by 2030 via ultra-mega solar parks (UMREPPs), SECI and state RE auctions, hybrid and floating solar, focused on Rajasthan, Gujarat and Maharashtra for solar and Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh for wind, plus captive solar and third-party sale under green open access. SGEL has 1460 MW of projects under operation; 855 MW is under construction (Bagodra 70 MW Gujarat, COD March-2027; GUVNL Phase-XIII 100 MW Gujarat, June-2027; GUVNL Phase-XIV 260 MW Gujarat, June-2027; Jamui Phase-I 75 MW Bihar, July 2026; APDCL 50 MW Assam, July 2026; GUVNL Phase-XVII Khavda 200 MW Gujarat, Dec 2026; RUVNL Nawa 100 MW Rajasthan, Sep 2026) and 1500 MW is under pre-construction (PSPSCL ET-2 100 MW Punjab, March 2027; PSPSCL ET-4 200 MW Punjab, March 2027; PSPSCL ET-3 1000 MW Pan India, March 2027; APDCL 200 MW Assam, December 2027). Under GUVNL Phase-XXII SJVN has secured a 200 MW solar project in Gujarat with a PPA at Rs 2.63/kWh signed by SGEL on 09.04.2024 and financial closure achieved; EPC awards have been placed for 150 MW and the remaining 50 MW is at tendering stage and yet to be awarded (the section heading in the report labels this item '50 MW' while the body states 200 MW secured). In thermal, one 660 MW unit of the 1320 MW Buxar Thermal Power Project (STPL) was commissioned on 14.11.2025 and Unit-II is expected to be commissioned during FY 2026-27. In green hydrogen, SJVN will establish pilot-scale hydrogen production using dedicated solar power especially in arid regions, with a 10-20 TPD demonstration facility and future scaling based on commercial viability, and has been nominated by the Ministry of Power as nodal agency for a green hydrogen project in Nepal. Estimated amount of contracts remaining to be executed on capital account rose to Rs 5,826.78 crore as at 31 March 2026 from Rs 2,277.12 crore a year earlier (named capital-commitments disclosure).

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body:
- **Quality of earnings:** FY26 PAT flattered by INR 679 cr prior-period true-up; underlying growth far lower than headline +22% revenue / +4% PAT suggests.
- **Receivables blow-up:** Trade receivables jumped to INR 1,299 cr (from INR 262 cr), unbilled debtors INR 906 cr (incl INR 776 cr tariff-order billing slipping into FY27) — working-capital and realization risk.
- **PPA cancellation risk:** ~9-10 GW awarded-but-unsigned at risk; DISCOM demand/config mismatch + falling tariffs.
- **Curtailment:** Bikaner ~120 MW curtailed pending SVR reactor (Oct-26); Khavda/Gujarat ~300 MW curtailment risk from delayed transmission/connectivity.
- **Loss-making subsidiaries** (SGEL, STPL) dragging consol; turnaround entirely dependent on FY27 ramp execution.
- **Tax step-up:** Sec 80-IA holiday expired for Rampur & KWPP → structurally higher tax.
- **Forex:** INR 206 cr exchange-variation hit (Nepal/external borrowing exposure).
- **Execution/geology:** Nepal hydro history of delays.

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body:
- The +308% Q4 PAT and +22% FY revenue are largely **non-recurring true-up artifacts** — not a clean growth signal.
- The growth story has **structurally downshifted**: from a 25 GW-by-2030 aspirant to a "consolidate what we have" posture. Re-rating thesis must be reset.
- SJVN's loss-making thermal/solar is a **timing problem** (PLF/CUF ramp + pre-COD cost charging), not necessarily a structural one — FY27 is the proof point.
- The REIA/aggregator model exposes SJVN to **DISCOM demand risk** it doesn't fully control — awarded GW ≠ contracted GW.
- Grid-balancing equipment (SVR reactors) is a **single-point bottleneck** ("limited manufacturer") capping solar output — a sector-wide integration constraint as solar penetration rises.
